ideas.original_title: B077. Sequential multi-risk control with prioritized actions
ideas.original_text:
Suppose a system can take several fallback actions in a fixed order. Once an early check fires, nothing reaches the later checks. Loosening the first threshold may therefore increase what the second stage has to handle. How can we choose all the thresholds so each action meets its own risk budget and the final policy is still useful? In our MultiRisk work, each risk averages its contribution over the whole stream of inputs. Conditioning only on the cases that reached a stage would give a different target. Yan, Hamed, Edgar and I studied how the priority order can be used in calibration.

Related work. Our MultiRisk paper uses priority to control several unconditional risk contributions simultaneously [reference in Storage], extending the single-loss calibration principle of conformal risk control [reference in Storage]. Learn then Test can evaluate families of candidate configurations under multiple risks [reference in Storage]; its high-probability certification differs from a marginal expected test-loss bound for the deployed recursion.

ideas.original_title: B078. MultiRisk: bumped empirical inverses and a symmetric threshold chain
ideas.original_text:
A tempting procedure is to choose the first threshold on the calibration sample, freeze it, and find the smallest second threshold whose empirical risk is acceptable. But the second loss now depends on a choice made using the same data. Can we still control its expected test loss? MultiRisk adds a worst-case test contribution to the empirical sum and works with slightly tightened risk levels. The proof compares the thresholds we can compute with auxiliary thresholds symmetric in the calibration and test points. The symmetry is how exchangeability enters. Only the thresholds learned from the calibration data are deployed.

Related work. Conformal risk control adds a worst-case contribution for the unobserved test loss before taking a single empirical inverse [reference in Storage]. MultiRisk uses several symmetric comparison thresholds because later losses depend on earlier fitted thresholds [reference in Storage]; the proof’s joint-sample thresholds are comparison devices, not extra test information needed for deployment.

ideas.original_title: B079. Tightness via anti-overshoot, weighted nesting, and jump counting
ideas.original_text:
If the procedure promises a risk below a budget, how far below it will we actually land? In a threshold problem, lowering the threshold by one step can move a whole block of observations across a boundary. An early move also changes which losses appear downstream. Our lower-bound argument keeps track of both effects. For score-based losses, absence of ties limits the jump at one threshold, and a nesting condition lets us charge downstream loss to the observations that moved earlier. Under those extra conditions the slack can be of order 1/n for a fixed number of stages. Upper control alone wouldn’t tell us that.

Related work. Conformal risk control derives a complementary lower bound when loss jumps do not pile up [reference in Storage]. MultiRisk has to count changes passed from one stage to later stages [reference in Storage]; near-tightness therefore uses assumptions on jumps and nesting beyond those sufficient for simultaneous upper control.

ideas.original_title: B080. Near-optimality from stable population inverses
ideas.original_text:
A feasible set of thresholds could leave a lot of useful predictions on the table. How does the calibrated objective compare with what we would choose if we knew the population risks? Two things have to go right. First, small errors in estimating risk must produce small changes in the thresholds. This depends on how the population risk crosses the budget at each stage. Second, the thresholds picked by the population recursion must themselves solve the decision problem we want to compare against. The draft separates these steps. A stability bound for the estimated recursion doesn’t establish the second claim.

Related work. Our MultiRisk preprint compares the fitted objective with a population minimizer under stated hypotheses. Lemma D.6 identifies when the population recursion solves its optimization problem, and Theorem 5.26 bounds the fitted objective under additional regularity [reference in Storage]. Bahadur’s quantile expansion gives a one-dimensional analogue for stability of the inverse [reference in Storage]. For a different utility I would check the population minimizer first, before trying to carry over the stability argument.

ideas.original_title: B081. Exact oracle recovery when scores have finite support
ideas.original_text:
For scores taking only finitely many values, two quite different numerical thresholds can induce exactly the same decisions. This suggests a simpler notion of stability. Suppose the budget lies strictly between two attainable risk levels at each stage of the population recursion. If the empirical risks are close enough, they pick out the very same threshold choices. We can then ask how many samples are needed to recover that population policy exactly. If a budget sits on a risk level, even a tiny sampling fluctuation can change the answer. Finite support on its own is insufficient.

Related work. MultiRisk gives the threshold recursion whose discrete decisions are to be recovered [reference in Storage]. For i.i.d. bounded losses, Hoeffding’s inequality and a union bound over the finite candidate risks give a direct baseline [reference in Storage]: a positive stagewise separation can preserve every comparison, whereas finite support alone supplies no separation.

ideas.original_title: B088. Rare-atom experiments exposing plug-in risk failures
ideas.original_text:
I wanted an example where the empirical risk looks reassuring for a perfectly understandable reason: a rare, expensive loss simply didn’t occur in the small calibration sample. The synthetic example puts a small probability on a large loss and routes cases through successive thresholds. The plug-in procedure can act as though the expensive outcome doesn’t exist. The worst-case correction can guard against it, but that protection also changes how many cases get through. The expectation-risk experiment and the earlier exceedance-probability experiment measure different things even when they use a similar mixture of ordinary and rare observations.

Related work. Conformal Risk Control adds a worst-case contribution for the unseen observation when calibrating a bounded, monotone loss [reference in Storage]. MultiRisk carries a related correction through a sequence of prioritized filters [reference in Storage]. The rare atom makes the cost of omitting that contribution observable even when the calibration sample contains no large loss.

ideas.original_title: B089. Synthetic scaling and fair baseline comparisons
ideas.original_text:
As the number of risk constraints grows, how much more conservative or expensive does calibration become? In the core synthetic example we can generate scores ourselves, set the budgets, and see exactly what fraction of cases the policy accepts. This makes comparisons with direct empirical thresholding and finite-grid testing easier to interpret. Here the fraction that passes all three filters is the objective loss, so smaller is better. LTT-Holm had lower values for all three stage risks but let 67.9% pass, compared with 47.0% for MultiRisk. I’d compare achieved risk, acceptance and calibration time together, keeping track of how finely each method was allowed to search. The six-constraint experiment asks how these tradeoffs change beyond the small three-score example.

Related work. MultiRisk uses the filter order to select thresholds recursively [reference in Storage]. Learn then Test certifies candidate settings through multiple testing [reference in Storage], while Pareto Testing screens settings before testing them on separate data [reference in Storage]. In this synthetic experiment the objective is to minimize the fraction passing every filter at the given stage-risk budgets. I would report that fraction alongside the number of threshold vectors each method considers.

ideas.original_title: B090. LLM abstention with safety and uncertainty scores
ideas.original_text:
When should an assistant abstain? In the PKU-SafeRLHF experiment we generated a response with Alpaca, used Llama Guard to score two groups of hazards, and used perplexity as a proxy for uncertainty. If a score crosses its threshold the assistant gives a fixed abstention response. We assigned a bounded cost to the answer it actually gives, using the Beaver reward model. For each abstention route, we average its reward-derived cost over all prompts, counting zero when that route is not taken. We likewise average the cost of the original answer times the indicator that we kept it. We report the fraction kept separately.

Related work. PKU-SafeRLHF records human judgments of response helpfulness and safety [reference in Storage]. Llama Guard supplies a separate model-based hazard classification [reference in Storage], and our MultiRisk experiment uses hazard scores to route responses [reference in Storage]. The comparison is the reward-derived cost contributed by each route, averaged over all prompts with zero contribution off that route. The kept-original objective is defined the same way. Keeping frequency is a separate outcome.

ideas.original_title: B091. Different LLM failures trigger different fallback outputs
ideas.original_text:
Abstention seems a blunt response to three different problems. If the first or second safety check fires, could the assistant regenerate an answer suited to that hazard? If uncertainty is the issue, could it give the answer with a qualification? We generated all four possible outputs before calibration, including the original answer. The checks use scores from the original, but the cost is the reward-based cost of the answer actually returned. With a budget of 0.20 for each of the three routes, the measured MultiRisk costs were 0.192, 0.117 and 0.170 in the representative experiment.

Related work. Our MultiRisk framework permits a different output modification at each stage of an ordered policy [reference in Storage]. Self-Refine gives a concrete example of improving an output through model-generated feedback and revision [reference in Storage]. To evaluate hazard-specific regeneration here, I would score the replacement itself and account for how often that branch is used.

ideas.original_title: B092. Fourteen-category scaling and score/assumption diagnostics
ideas.original_text:
What happens as we give each safety category its own threshold? We increased the number of active Llama Guard categories from three to fourteen. Giving each category the same budget is quite different from dividing a fixed total among all of them, especially when some hazards are rare. At the representative fourteen-category setting, with a budget of 0.20 per category, MultiRisk abstained on about half the prompts. Some score distributions were highly concentrated. Looking at the mass near the chosen thresholds could help explain why changing a threshold sometimes has little effect and sometimes moves many responses at once.

Related work. Llama Guard 3 defines fourteen hazard categories that can supply separate routing signals [reference in Storage]. The priority ordering in MultiRisk [reference in Storage] and the candidate screening in Pareto Testing [reference in Storage] give two ways to manage many constraints. A comparison has to specify whether each new category receives a fresh budget or a share of a fixed total.

ideas.original_text:
Can a classifier stop at an intermediate layer when the rest of the network would add little? On AG News we fitted probes at eleven layers of BERT. An early exit incurs a loss if the probe is wrong on an example the full classifier would have gotten right. With a representative per-stage budget of 0.020, MultiRisk used about a fifth of the full compute. Its accuracy was 0.911, compared with 0.952 for the full classifier. Limiting each route’s contribution to excess error can still cost several points of accuracy overall.

Related work. DeeBERT lets an example exit at an intermediate classifier [reference in Storage], and Jazbec et al. calibrate early exits against a specified quality loss [reference in Storage]. MultiRisk supplies separate risk budgets across the ordered exits [reference in Storage]. The experiment here budgets the contribution of each layer to errors the full classifier would have avoided.

ideas.original_title: B094. Audit total output quality separately from the calibrated objective
ideas.original_text:
Does optimizing the quantity we calibrated improve the answer someone actually receives? In our LLM abstention experiment, MultiRisk had the smaller calibrated objective, but the Beaver reward model gave its outputs lower quality scores than those from Learn then Test with Holm correction. We saw a much smaller quality gap in the intervention experiment. Beaver was also part of the evaluation, so an independent judge could rank the outputs differently. The early-exit experiment gives us a cleaner check of overall classification accuracy because we have the true labels.

Related work. Gao et al. compare a proxy reward with a separate reference reward as optimization pressure grows and find that the two can diverge [reference in Storage]. Our MultiRisk procedure controls the particular routed losses supplied to calibration [reference in Storage]. A separate judgment of all returned responses would tell us whether the ranking survives a change of evaluator as well as a change of objective.

ideas.original_title: B082. VaR control by reducing losses to exceedance indicators
ideas.original_text:
What if the deployment requirement is about a bad outcome in the tail, rather than the mean loss? The (1 − α)-quantile is at most β exactly when the probability that loss exceeds β is at most α. We can feed the indicator of exceedance into the expectation-risk procedure. For a sequence of fallback actions we must check that this transformation keeps the monotonicity and feasible endpoints the recursion needs. The resulting target is the marginal tail probability on a new case. A particular calibration sample may do better or worse.

Related work. MultiRisk supplies the expectation-risk recursion once each loss is replaced by its exceedance indicator [reference in Storage]. Quantile Learn-Then-Test [reference in Storage] and quantile risk control [reference in Storage] offer comparisons based on high-confidence population-quantile guarantees. The quantity to compare here is the marginal exceedance probability of the deployed priority rule, including calibration randomness.

ideas.original_title: B083. General quantile-based risks from finite bundles of VaR constraints
ideas.original_text:
An upper bound on one quantile says little about the rest of the tail. Could we control a weighted average of quantiles by bounding exceedance probabilities at several loss levels? For bounded nonnegative losses, the risk can be written as an integral of a function of the tail probabilities. Before calibration, choose a grid whose last point bounds the loss almost surely and assign exceedance budgets at the left endpoints so the resulting upper sum stays within the risk budget. The stage threshold has to satisfy every component. A finer grid better approximates the integral, while the choice of how much budget to give each component still matters.

Related work. Snell et al. bound quantile-based risks using confidence bounds on the loss distribution [reference in Storage]. Here the calibration primitive is instead MultiRisk [reference in Storage]: a predetermined finite bundle of exceedance constraints has to imply the tail-integral bound and remain feasible at each stage of the priority recursion.

ideas.original_title: B084. CVaR budget allocation: constant, linear, and power profiles
ideas.original_text:
For CVaR we care about the average size of losses in the upper tail. In the finite-grid approach, we can give every loss level the same exceedance budget. We could instead allow more exceedances at moderate losses and make the very largest losses rarer. Which allocation leaves the most useful decisions available while still bounding the tail average? The draft compares equal budgets with decreasing profiles, including a linear profile. Those options change the conservatism of the bound. They must be chosen in a way consistent with how the calibration data will be used.

Related work. Rockafellar and Uryasev express CVaR using an auxiliary threshold and expected excess loss [reference in Storage]; quantile risk control bounds tail functionals from distributional information [reference in Storage], and conformal risk training gives an OCE-based alternative [reference in Storage]. These are comparisons for the cost of replacing the tail integral with a finite grid and allocating its budgets before calibration.

ideas.original_title: B087. High-probability sequential QRC using disjoint calibration splits
ideas.original_text:
The marginal guarantee averages over the calibration sample and the next test case. What if we want high confidence, after drawing the calibration data, that all the population risks meet their budgets? One simple two-stage route is to split the data. Choose the first threshold on the first split, then calibrate the second on observations the first choice hasn’t seen. A finite set of candidates lets us account for the search and the two risk statements. The cost is fewer observations at each stage and a penalty for considering many candidates. This was a preliminary approach to the stronger guarantee.

Related work. Learn then Test uses a held-out sample to test which candidate settings meet population risk targets with high confidence [reference in Storage]. Quantile Risk Control constructs confidence bounds from loss order statistics, including bounds for tail functionals [reference in Storage]. In the two-stage sketch, the question is how much the second bound costs once the first threshold has been selected on a separate split.

ideas.original_title: B095. Tail-risk experiment continuation and reproducibility
ideas.original_text:
The expectation-risk experiments leave open what happens in the tail of the loss distribution. I would like to keep the same abstention and intervention tasks, the same splits and the same competing methods, then ask how much answering or routing costs at a specified upper quantile. For conditional value at risk, how does dividing the budget equally across the component constraints compare with allowing unequal allocations? The tail-risk draft describes the comparisons and the planned plots. The numerical tables from the expectation-risk experiments answer a different question.

Related work. Snell et al. bound loss quantiles using order statistics [reference in Storage], and Rockafellar and Uryasev give an auxiliary-threshold representation of CVaR [reference in Storage]. Applying these ideas to the ordered policies of MultiRisk [reference in Storage] would require evaluating the loss distribution of each selected policy. The reported means on the existing splits do not determine its upper tail.
